notes: ML.ENERGY paper (2505.06371v2) reports energy mainly PER GENERATION (per response) by design (Sec. 2.3); per-token values in the paper are only implicit (Eq. 2: E_req = E_steady/Tokens_steady x mean output tokens). It measures GPU energy only (Zeus/NVML).

The ONLY prefill/decode split in the ML.ENERGY paper is Appendix B.3 Table 4 (PD disaggregation: J/generation + % decode energy). Our per-token prefill/decode values from it are DERIVED as ratio of means (dataset means, not realised sample means) and flagged approx=true. GPU type for Table 4 is not stated.

Table 4 context evidence: Llama-3.1-8B 1P3D decode J/out-token = 0.0569 (in512/out512), 0.1604 (in512/out4096), 0.2727 (in4096/out512). But configs with the same mean decode KV length (~4608) differ widely (long-output vs long-input: 8B 1P3D 0.160 vs 0.273; 8B 2P2D 0.170 vs 0.164; 70B 1P1D 0.198 vs 1.458), and for 70B the long-output case is even BELOW the 512/512 case (0.350). Batch/serving dynamics and PD-instance balance dominate, so Table 4 alone cannot identify e_dec(ctx)=a+b*ctx.

ML.ENERGY Leaderboard data used is the CURRENT v3 release (H100 & B200, vLLM; tasks lm-arena-chat, gpqa), files from github.com/ml-energy/leaderboard commit 2bdd0070186956688e1f842dc28077980fe64013 (committed 2026-09-23). This is NEWER than the early-2025 (A100/H100) iteration described in the paper; numbers differ from the paper's figures. energy_per_token_joules = steady-state GPU energy / output tokens (prefill energy included, not separable). No prompt-length field is present in these JSONs.

Raw per-run data (timelines, prompt lengths) is in the ML.ENERGY data toolkit / HF dataset (github.com/ml-energy/data, pip mlenergy-data, LLMRuns.from_hf()); NOT downloaded here. That is the best route to a genuine e_dec(ctx) fit from ML.ENERGY.

TokenPowerBench (2512.03024v1): hardware 8 nodes x 4 H100 (94 GB). Prefill/decode attribution is claimed by the tool, but the paper only shows Fig. 2(a) prefill energy with an UNLABELED unit (log axis 1k-25k, not per token) and Fig. 2(b) per-token values whose caption says 'Decode Energy per Token' while the text says 'total energy per token'. No tables of numbers; 'supplementary material' with full results was not found in the arXiv HTML/PDF.

TokenPowerBench Fig. 2/3 values were read by pixel measurement of the PDF render (720 dpi) against the log-scale gridlines extracted from the PDF vector data: approximate, roughly +-5%. Fig. 4 values come from vector marker coordinates (more precise). Fig. 5 and Fig. 6 values are printed numbers in the figure.

INCONSISTENCY in TokenPowerBench: text says Llama3-70B energy/token rises ~3x from 2K to 10K prompt tokens, but Fig. 3(a) bars give ~0.87 (0-2K) -> ~1.2 J/token (5-10K), i.e. ~1.4x. Fig. 5 (405B TP16 SL 163.1, HC 177.3, HT 191.2) and Fig. 6 FP16 (SL 177, HC 192, HT 207; TP16-PP1 177) also do not match each other exactly.

Magnitude caveat: TokenPowerBench 405B/180B/480B values are 100-290 'J/token' on 16 H100 - ~100x higher than ML.ENERGY's Llama-3.1-405B (~1-22 J/token on 8xB200) and implausible as per-output-token at batch 128-1024; TPB small-model values (e.g. Llama3-8B vLLM ~0.15 J/token) are in line with ML.ENERGY. Treat TPB large-model numbers as possibly using a different normalisation (e.g. per request or per batch-step); do not use them for e_dec calibration without checking the code.

Context scaling statements (quotes) - TokenPowerBench, 'Context Length' subsection (Fig. 3): 'Across all models, energy grows steadily as the prompt gets longer because the prefill stage must process every input token while the compute cost of each new output token stays the same.' ; 'For the largest dense model we tested (Llama3 70B), the jump from 2K to 10 K tokens raises energy per token by roughly a factor of three; medium models (e.g., Llama 3 8B, Mistral 7B) see a smaller but still clear rise.' ; 'Longer prompts therefore hurt energy efficiency in two ways: they increase the joules spent before the first output token appears, and they lower overall throughput because GPUs stay busy on attention over a larger context window.' ; Execution and Measurement / 2) Temporal view: 'This separation reveals, for instance, that long prompts raise the prefill share, while large batch sizes increase the decode share.' NOTE: TPB asserts per-output-token decode compute 'stays the same' with context - i.e. it does NOT model attention/KV growth in decode.

Context scaling statements - ML.ENERGY paper: App. B.3: 'Overall, decode consumes the majority of energy, with some amount shifting to prefill when input length is long.' ; Sec. 4.2: 'Reasoning models produce one to two orders of magnitude more output tokens per request ... due to their long output lengths, servers cannot run as large a batch size, preventing them from amortizing energy across more requests. This leads to higher energy per token as well' ; Sec. 4.2: 'Mini's KV cache uses 3x more memory than Small, which prevents it from scaling to larger batch sizes and amortizing energy consumption across more generations.' ; App. C: 'Prefill has high compute-intensity (and also high power draw) ... whereas Decode has low compute-intensity (and low power draw)'. ML.ENERGY attributes context effects mainly to KV-memory-limited batch size, not per-token attention FLOPs.

Other TPB text numbers: Llama-3 1B->70B energy/token x7.3 (Cross-Model section); Mixtral-8x7B ~ dense 8B energy/token; TensorRT-LLM & vLLM ~3x more prefill energy than DeepSpeed/Transformers but 25-40% less energy/token than Transformers; FP8 cuts Llama-3 405B energy/token ~30% (45 kJ -> 32 kJ per batch, heaviest load); batch 32->256 cuts 70B energy/token ~25%.

Indirect leaderboard context evidence: Qwen3-8B on 1xH100 at max_num_seqs=64: 0.119 J/tok on lm-arena-chat (avg out 645 tok) vs 0.267 J/tok on GPQA (avg out 8367 tok). Confounded by different prompts/task and by realised batch; recorded in context_scaling with ctx proxy = avg_output_len/2.
